questions.question: Giardia belongs to which family?
questions.explanation: Giardia belongs to the family Hexamitidae — flagellated protozoa with bilaterally symmetrical bodies. Entamoebidae contains amoebae; the other two families contain entirely different parasites.

questions.question: How many Giardia species are considered valid and of importance?
questions.explanation: Five Giardia species are considered valid: G. duodenalis (the human pathogen), G. muris, G. agilis, G. psittaci, and G. ardeae. The others infect animals and are not human pathogens.

questions.question: Giardia duodenalis was first discovered by whom?
questions.explanation: Giardia duodenalis was first observed by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in 1681 — the same Dutch microscopist who first saw bacteria. He found it in his own stool.

questions.question: In which year was Giardia duodenalis first discovered?
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek's discovery of Giardia dates to 1681 — one of the earliest microscopic observations of a protozoan parasite.

questions.question: Giardia duodenalis is cosmopolitan but occurs especially in which climates?
questions.explanation: Giardia is cosmopolitan but occurs especially in warm climates, where contaminated water and poor sanitation facilitate transmission.

questions.question: Which group is most susceptible to Giardia infection?
questions.explanation: Children are most susceptible to Giardia infection, particularly in daycare settings and areas with poor sanitation. They shed more cysts and have less developed hygiene habits.

questions.question: Giardiasis is transmitted by swallowing what?
questions.explanation: Giardiasis is transmitted by swallowing mature, infective cysts — usually in contaminated water or food. Trophozoites cannot survive the stomach acid and are not infective.

questions.question: The prevalence of Giardia infection ranges from 2.4% to what percentage?
questions.explanation: Global prevalence of Giardia infection ranges from 2.4% to 67.5%, varying widely with sanitation, water quality, and local epidemiology.

questions.question: Which wild animal is epidemiologically significant in human giardiasis?
questions.explanation: Beavers are epidemiologically significant — they carry G. duodenalis and contaminate water sources. "Beaver fever" is a colloquial name for giardiasis.

questions.question: Giardiasis can also be what type of disease?
questions.explanation: Giardiasis can also be a zoonosis — some strains of G. duodenalis infect both animals and humans, allowing transmission from animals to people.

questions.question: The trophozoites of Giardia are shaped like what?
questions.explanation: Giardia trophozoites are pear-shaped (pyriform) — bilaterally symmetrical, with a broad anterior end and tapering posterior end.

questions.question: How many flagella does Giardia trophozoite have?
questions.explanation: The Giardia trophozoite has eight flagella — arranged as four pairs (anterior, posterior-lateral, ventral, and caudal). They provide the characteristic "falling leaf" motility.

questions.question: Giardia trophozoite lacks which organelle?
questions.explanation: Giardia trophozoites lack mitochondria — they are anaerobic and derive energy from fermentation. This is a distinguishing feature of the parasite.

questions.question: Giardia lives in which part of the human body?
questions.explanation: Giardia lives in the duodenum, jejunum, and upper ileum — where it attaches to the intestinal mucosa and interferes with absorption.

questions.question: Trophozoites of Giardia divide by what process?
questions.explanation: Giardia trophozoites divide by binary fission (longitudinal), multiplying rapidly in the small intestine.

questions.question: Giardia encysts in which part of the intestine?
questions.explanation: Giardia encysts in the colon, where the environment is drier and the parasites are exposed to the forming faecal mass. Cysts are then passed in stool.

questions.question: The cyst of Giardia measures how many micrometers?
questions.explanation: Giardia cysts measure about 8 to 12 µm long by 7 to 10 µm wide — oval, with a smooth wall and distinctive internal structures.

questions.question: Newly formed Giardia cysts have how many nuclei?
questions.explanation: Newly formed cysts have two nuclei, which then divide to produce four nuclei as the cyst matures.

questions.question: Older Giardia cysts have how many nuclei?
questions.explanation: Mature (older) cysts contain four nuclei — the infective stage when swallowed. After excystation, each nucleus gives rise to a trophozoite.

questions.question: Giardia infection causes increased production of what?
questions.explanation: Giardia infection causes increased mucus production in the small intestine — the intestinal mucosa responds to the parasite's presence with hypersecretion.

questions.question: Giardia infection leads to non-absorption of what?
questions.explanation: Giardia infection leads to malabsorption of fats and other nutrients — the parasite damages the brush border and interferes with absorption, causing steatorrhoea and weight loss.

questions.question: Jaundice in Giardia infection occurs by infestation of what?
questions.explanation: Jaundice in Giardia infection occurs when the parasite infests the gallbladder, obstructing the bile duct and causing cholestatic jaundice.

questions.question: Diagnosis of Giardia is by demonstration of what in stained fecal smears?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis is by demonstration of trophozoites and cysts in stained fecal smears. Trophozoites are found in fresh watery stool, cysts in formed stool.

questions.question: Giardia treatment is most effective with quinacrine or what?
questions.explanation: Giardia treatment is most effective with quinacrine or metronidazole. Metronidazole is generally preferred because of better tolerance and fewer side effects.

questions.question: To avoid re-infection, who should be treated simultaneously?
questions.explanation: To avoid re-infection, all household members should be treated simultaneously — otherwise an untreated family member can reinfect the patient through shared food, water, or hygiene contacts.
